questions.prompt: Which change most directly makes a soluble protein surface less favorable in water?
options: Replacing exposed polar residues with nonpolar residues
Adding ionizable side chains at neutral pH
Increasing the number of backbone hydrogen bonds
Reducing the protein's molecular mass without changing sequence

variants.prompt: A soluble enzyme acquires a surface mutation. Which substitution is most likely to make hydration of that surface less favorable?
options: Replace several exposed polar residues with leucine
Replace exposed leucine residues with serine
Add ionizable side chains that are charged at the buffer pH
Add polar side chains that can hydrogen-bond with water

feedback.hint: Compare the ability of each side chain to make favorable interactions with water.
feedback.solution: Leucine is nonpolar. Replacing exposed polar residues with leucine increases nonpolar surface area and makes hydration less favorable; the effect on aggregation depends on the rest of the protein and conditions.

variants.prompt: A folded cytosolic protein is engineered to expose a larger nonpolar surface area. Which prediction follows most directly from the hydrophobic effect?
options: Water forms more hydrogen bonds directly with the nonpolar surface
Hydration is less favorable, which can favor burial or association of that surface
The exposed groups must form new covalent bonds with neighboring proteins
Solubility is determined by protein molecular mass alone

feedback.hint: Focus on solvent interactions and distinguish a thermodynamic tendency from a guaranteed cellular outcome.
feedback.solution: Water cannot make the usual hydrogen-bond interactions with a nonpolar surface. Increasing exposed nonpolar area makes hydration less favorable and can favor burial or association, though it does not by itself prove aggregation in a particular cell.

feedback.hint: Think about which groups can make favorable interactions with water.
feedback.solution: Nonpolar surface area disrupts water's hydrogen-bond network. Exposing more nonpolar residues raises the free-energy cost of hydration and can promote aggregation or burial in a folded state.

questions.prompt: Opening a selective K⁺ channel changes membrane potential. Which statement is most accurate?
options: K⁺ moves until its electrochemical potential difference is zero
K⁺ must move until both sides have equal K⁺ concentrations
ATP is consumed by each K⁺ passing through the channel
The channel changes the total amount of K⁺ in the cell without flux

feedback.hint: Balance the concentration and electrical contributions; equal concentrations are not required.
feedback.solution: At electrochemical equilibrium the chemical and electrical contributions cancel. An ion channel is passive and does not itself hydrolyze ATP; a concentration difference can remain at the Nernst potential.

questions.prompt: An enzyme has Vmax = 120 μmol·min⁻¹ and Km = 3 mM. What rate is predicted at [S] = 6 mM? Enter the numerical value in μmol·min⁻¹.

feedback.hint: Substitute [S] and Km into v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]).
feedback.solution: v = 120 × 6/(3 + 6) = 80 μmol·min⁻¹. The substrate concentration is twice Km, so the enzyme is approaching saturation but is not at Vmax.

questions.prompt: A PCR band is absent in a treated sample. Which control most directly shows the PCR itself could detect the target?
options: A positive control containing target template
A second untreated sample with no template
A loading dye-only lane
A replicate of the treated sample

feedback.hint: Choose a condition expected to produce the signal if the assay works.
feedback.solution: A positive control with target template tests reagent and assay performance. A no-template control is useful for contamination but cannot establish that target amplification is possible.

questions.prompt: Which statements best explain how amphipathic phospholipids form a bilayer in water? Select all that apply.
options: Nonpolar acyl chains are largely shielded from water in the bilayer interior.
Polar headgroups remain hydrated at the membrane surfaces.
The lipids must form new covalent bonds before they can assemble.
Lipids can form ordered assemblies in water without an enzyme catalyzing a covalent reaction.
Hydrophobic tails are stabilized by favorable ionic bonds with water.

feedback.hint: Account for both the nonpolar tails and the polar headgroups in their aqueous environment.
feedback.solution: The hydrophobic effect favors reducing contact between nonpolar tails and water while polar headgroups stay hydrated. Self-assembly is driven by noncovalent interactions and does not require an enzyme to make covalent bonds. The score uses max(0, correct selections minus incorrect selections) divided by three, multiplied by three points.

questions.prompt: Build an experiment-and-inference chain for a candidate transcription regulator by answering each explicit analytic criterion.

response_fields.prompt: Control fidelity · Which condition controls for sequence-independent delivery effects?
options: A non-targeting oligonucleotide delivered with the same reagent and timing.
Untreated cells with no delivery reagent.
A knockdown of an unrelated essential gene.
More replicates of the candidate-regulator knockdown alone.

response_fields.prompt: Direct occupancy · Which result tests whether the regulator occupies the target promoter?
options: Validated promoter enrichment by ChIP-qPCR compared with an appropriate assay control.
A lower target-RNA measurement after regulator depletion.
A western blot confirming that the regulator's abundance decreased.
A single endpoint image with no locus-specific measurement.

response_fields.prompt: Cis-regulatory test · Which comparison asks whether the candidate motif mediates the transcription response?
options: Matched reporter constructs with the intact versus mutated candidate binding motif.
A second endpoint measurement of the same bulk RNA sample.
An unrelated promoter reporter measured in a different cell line.
A replicate of the depleted condition without a matched reporter control.

response_fields.prompt: Inference boundary · What claim is supported by controlled depletion, rescue, and direct-regulation evidence?
options: The regulator contributes to expression in this tested system and condition; broader scope requires additional evidence.
The regulator is necessary in every cell type and condition.
The regulator alone is sufficient to set expression in every tissue.
The observed association proves that no other regulator contributes.

evidence: The control matches delivery reagent and timing while omitting the target sequence.
Locus enrichment is compared against an assay control; expression change alone does not show binding.
Matched intact and motif-mutated constructs isolate the candidate binding site.
The conclusion is limited to the tested cells and conditions.

feedback.hint: Separate a delivery control, a binding assay, a motif-dependence test, and the scope of the causal claim.
feedback.solution: A matched non-targeting oligonucleotide tests delivery effects. Controlled promoter enrichment addresses occupancy, a motif-mutant reporter tests cis-regulatory dependence, and rescue strengthens attribution in the tested system without establishing a universal rule.

questions.prompt: From this original two-condition dataset (normalized signal): vehicle = 4.8, 5.2, 5.0, 5.0; inhibitor = 2.6, 2.8, 2.7, 2.9. Upload a UTF-8 CSV with exactly these columns in order: condition, replicate_count, mean_signal. Include one row each named vehicle and inhibitor. Compute the replicate count and arithmetic mean, rounding means to two decimal places. This formative check scores the submitted summary cells only; it does not grade a causal interpretation.

evidence: The vehicle summary row reports all four supplied replicates.
The vehicle mean is the arithmetic average of the four supplied values.
The inhibitor summary row reports all four supplied replicates.
The inhibitor mean is the arithmetic average of the four supplied values.

feedback.hint: Group the replicate observations by condition, then report the number of observations and arithmetic mean for each group.
feedback.solution: The vehicle count is 4 and its mean is 5.00. The inhibitor count is 4 and its mean is 2.75. These two descriptive means alone do not establish statistical significance or a causal effect.

questions.prompt: A solvent-exposed glutamate is replaced by glutamine at pH 7.4. Which prediction best follows from the chemical change without overclaiming a phenotype?
options: A usually negative carboxylate is replaced by a polar amide, so a local electrostatic interaction may change and should be measured.
The mutation removes the peptide backbone and guarantees that no protein is made.
The mutation creates a disulfide bond with any nearby cysteine.
The mutation makes the side chain nonpolar and unable to contact water.

feedback.hint: Compare the side-chain charge near neutral pH while remembering that both groups can interact with water.
feedback.solution: Glutamate is usually negatively charged near pH 7.4, whereas glutamine is a polar, uncharged amide. A local electrostatic effect is plausible, but the sequence change alone does not prove loss of expression or function.

questions.prompt: For a simple carboxyl group with pKa 5.0, approximately what fraction is deprotonated at pH 6.0 under the Henderson-Hasselbalch model?
options: About 91 percent
About 50 percent
About 9 percent
About 1 percent

feedback.hint: One pH unit above pKa gives a tenfold excess of deprotonated over protonated form.
feedback.solution: The ratio [A-]/[HA] is 10, so the deprotonated fraction is 10/(10+1), about 0.91. This is a simple two-state model; local protein environments can shift pKa.

questions.prompt: A membrane protein couples sodium moving down its electrochemical gradient to glucose moving uphill. How should the glucose movement be classified?
options: Secondary active cotransport
Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer
Passive facilitated diffusion down the glucose gradient
Primary active transport directly coupled to ATP hydrolysis by this protein

feedback.hint: Identify which solute moves downhill and whether the transporter directly uses ATP.
feedback.solution: The downhill sodium gradient supplies energy for uphill glucose transport, which is secondary active cotransport. The protein is energy-coupled but does not directly hydrolyze ATP in the stated mechanism.

questions.prompt: Analyze a buried leucine-to-aspartate protein substitution. Make a bounded prediction, select measurements that distinguish its mechanism, and limit the scope of the inference.

response_fields.prompt: Mechanistic prediction: which statement is justified from the sequence change alone?
options: Reduced stability is plausible, but complete loss of expression or activity is not established.
The protein must be absent from every cell because a buried charge cannot be tolerated.
The substitution proves that the protein binds a new substrate.
No effect is possible because both residues occur in proteins.

response_fields.prompt: Discriminating evidence: which measurement set best separates abundance, folding, and catalytic explanations?
options: Compare abundance and soluble fraction, test folding, and measure specific activity at matched protein concentration.
Measure only the variant transcript once and infer its enzyme activity.
Repeat the DNA sequence and assume that it predicts cellular function.
Compare cell growth without measuring protein or activity.

response_fields.prompt: Inference scope: what conclusion is appropriate after a reproducible effect in one cell assay?
options: The variant affects the measured property in the tested system; broader phenotypes need additional evidence.
The variant has the same effect in every tissue and organism.
The assay proves the exact atomic structure of the protein.
The effect establishes clinical causation without genetic or clinical evidence.

evidence: Destabilization is presented as plausible rather than inevitable.
Abundance, folding or solubility, and activity at matched protein amount are distinguished.
The claim is limited to the tested measurement and system.

feedback.hint: Separate what the substitution makes plausible from what requires measurement; compare abundance, folding, and activity.
feedback.solution: A buried charge can destabilize a soluble-protein core, but it does not prove the protein is absent. Matched abundance and solubility measurements, folding-sensitive evidence, and specific activity at equal protein concentration distinguish candidate mechanisms. Any causal claim remains limited to the assay and cell context.

questions.prompt: A soluble protein has a cleavable N-terminal ER signal sequence. Which route best describes its common path to secretion?
options: SRP recognizes the emerging signal, the ribosome is targeted to an ER translocon, the protein enters the ER lumen, then cargo passes through Golgi and a secretory vesicle before release.
The completed protein enters the nucleus, exits through a nuclear pore, and crosses directly through the plasma-membrane lipid bilayer.
The protein is imported into the mitochondrial matrix and then carried by COPII vesicles to the Golgi.
The protein remains in the cytosol until a clathrin coat pulls it through the ER membrane.

feedback.hint: Separate translocation into the ER from later vesicle transport between lumenal compartments.
feedback.solution: An ER signal sequence is commonly recognized during translation and directs the ribosome–nascent-chain complex to an ER translocon. The soluble cargo enters the ER lumen and then moves through the Golgi and secretory vesicles. Vesicles carry cargo between compartments; they do not pull a soluble protein through a lipid bilayer.

questions.prompt: Interpret the synthetic protease-protection experiment and state what the controls allow you to conclude.

response_fields.prompt: Membrane-enclosure inference: wild-type signal is protected by protease in intact microsomes, while the signal-deletion construct is not. The ER-lumen marker is protected and the cytosolic marker is digested. Which inference is best supported?
options: The wild-type test protein entered a membrane-enclosed lumen; the deleted region is needed for entry under these conditions.
The signal-deletion construct is never translated in any cell.
The wild-type protein is proven to bind directly to a specific ER receptor.
The wild-type protein is localized specifically to the Golgi rather than the ER.

response_fields.prompt: Membrane-integrity control: what does adding detergent before protease contribute?
options: It opens the microsome membrane; loss of protection supports a membrane-dependent barrier to protease.
It proves that the protein binds SRP with a particular affinity.
It establishes that the tagged protein is enzymatically active.
It shows that all microsomes came from a single organelle.

response_fields.prompt: Inference boundary: which conclusion still requires additional measurements?
options: Which precise step—signal recognition, ribosome targeting, translocon engagement, or translocation—fails in the mutant.
Whether detergent changed access of protease to a lumenal marker.
Whether the wild-type signal is more protected than the signal-deletion construct in the stated assay.
Whether the cytosolic marker was exposed to protease in intact microsomes.

evidence: Infers membrane-enclosed lumenal access from protection and matched marker behavior.
Uses detergent to test whether membrane disruption removes protection.
Does not identify an unmeasured molecular import step.

feedback.hint: Use the ER-lumen and cytosolic markers to check assay behavior, then distinguish a localization inference from a molecular mechanism.
feedback.solution: Wild-type protection in intact microsomes, sensitivity after detergent, a protected lumenal marker, and a digested cytosolic marker support entry into a membrane-enclosed lumen. The signal-deletion result is consistent with impaired entry in this assay. It does not distinguish signal recognition from targeting, translocon engagement, or translocation; matched synthesis, time-course, and orthogonal localization evidence would narrow those possibilities.

questions.prompt: A cytosolic-tail mutant of the mannose-6-phosphate receptor binds cargo normally, but less newly synthesized cathepsin D reaches the lysosome fraction. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: A post-binding sorting or routing step is impaired; receptor abundance, compartment access, and fraction recovery still need checking.
The receptor cannot recognize mannose-6-phosphate because cargo binding is unchanged.
All lysosomal hydrolases are made directly inside the lysosome and bypass the Golgi.
The result proves that the tail binds one specific coat protein in every cell type.

feedback.hint: Separate cargo recognition from the later step that packages or routes the receptor–cargo complex.
feedback.solution: Preserved ligand binding with reduced lysosomal delivery is consistent with a defect after cargo recognition, such as sorting or routing. Receptor abundance, compartment localization, cargo synthesis, degradation, and fraction recovery are alternative explanations that need controls; the pattern does not identify a unique adaptor or establish a universal mechanism.

questions.prompt: A lumenal ER protein with a terminal KDEL sequence is detected transiently in an early Golgi compartment and later returns to the ER. What model best explains this observation?
options: A cycling receptor can retrieve escaped cargo from post-ER compartments; KDEL does not mean the protein is physically trapped in the ER at all times.
KDEL is an irreversible covalent anchor that prevents the protein from leaving the ER.
The protein must cross the Golgi membrane into the cytosol and then re-enter the ER.
The KDEL sequence converts the protein into a COPII coat subunit.

feedback.hint: Interpret the transient Golgi signal as evidence about movement, not permanent immobilization.
feedback.solution: KDEL is a retrieval signal for many soluble ER-resident proteins. Cargo can escape to post-ER compartments and be returned through receptor-mediated traffic. The magnitude and kinetics depend on the cargo and cellular context, so the tag is not an absolute, irreversible tether.

questions.prompt: A catalyst is added to a reversible reaction in a closed system. Which statement is correct under the same conditions?
options: It can accelerate approach to equilibrium without changing the equilibrium constant.
It makes the forward reaction favorable by changing the reaction ΔG°.
It speeds the forward reaction but must slow the reverse reaction.
It changes the equilibrium ratio whenever it lowers an activation barrier.

feedback.hint: Separate the barrier crossed on the way to equilibrium from the free-energy difference between reactants and products.
feedback.solution: A catalyst provides a lower-barrier pathway and can accelerate both forward and reverse reactions. It does not change the reaction free-energy difference or equilibrium constant.

questions.prompt: A cellular transformation has ΔG = +12.0 kJ/mol and a second reaction has ΔG = -21.0 kJ/mol under the stated conditions. If one event of each is physically coupled in a 1:1 mechanism, what is the net ΔG? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Add the two free-energy changes only because the prompt states that the reaction events are physically coupled.
feedback.solution: The net change is +12.0 + (-21.0) = -9.0 kJ/mol for the coupled process. Summing unrelated reactions would not establish cellular coupling.

questions.prompt: An enzyme preparation contains 20 nM active sites and has kcat = 4 s^-1. Under the simple model, what initial rate is predicted when [S] = Km? Enter a value in nM/s.

feedback.hint: First calculate Vmax = kcat × active-enzyme concentration; at [S] = Km the rate is half that value.
feedback.solution: Vmax = 4 s^-1 × 20 nM = 80 nM/s. At [S] = Km, v0 = Vmax/2 = 40 nM/s.

questions.prompt: A synthetic control dataset is modeled with Vmax = 120 nM/s and Km = 20 μM. What initial rate does the Michaelis–Menten equation predict at [S] = 40 μM? Enter a value in nM/s.

feedback.hint: Substitute the substrate concentration into v0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); keep the substrate units matched.
feedback.solution: v0 = 120 × 40/(20 + 40) = 80 nM/s. This is a model prediction at the specified conditions, not an additional measurement.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the synthetic initial-rate comparison in the week-4 lesson. Select one response for each criterion.

response_fields.prompt: Kinetic pattern · Which simple model pattern best matches lower rates at matched [S] with increasing convergence at high [S]?
options: A competitive-like pattern: apparent Km rises while the limiting Vmax may remain similar.
A pure uncompetitive pattern: both apparent Km and Vmax rise by the same factor.
An obligatory irreversible pattern: the data prove permanent enzyme destruction.
No model can compare rates measured at different substrate concentrations.

response_fields.prompt: Detector control · Which test directly checks whether the compound distorts the optical product readout?
options: Add inhibitor to a known product standard without enzyme and compare signal recovery with the matched vehicle.
Measure only a later endpoint at a single substrate concentration.
Increase enzyme concentration without checking the signal calibrator.
Replace the matched vehicle control with an untreated well.

response_fields.prompt: Inference boundary · What conclusion is justified by this synthetic curve pattern alone?
options: It is consistent with a competitive-like kinetic model, but does not prove a physical binding site or exclude alternatives.
The inhibitor must occupy the substrate-binding pocket in every cell type.
The unchanged high-substrate rate is directly measured as an exact Vmax.
The inhibitor cannot affect enzyme conformation or product release.

evidence: Identifies competitive-like behavior as increased apparent Km with a similar possible limiting Vmax, while describing it as a model pattern.
Uses a known product standard plus inhibitor without enzyme and compares signal recovery to matched vehicle.
States that curve shape is consistent with, but does not prove, a binding-site mechanism or exclude alternatives.

feedback.hint: Separate a rate-pattern description from a direct binding claim. Then choose the control that isolates the detector rather than the enzyme.
feedback.solution: The synthetic values are compatible with a competitive-like pattern, but the curve does not locate the inhibitor physically. A product standard with inhibitor and no enzyme tests optical interference against matched vehicle. Broader substrate and inhibitor ranges, parameter uncertainty, and orthogonal binding or recovery experiments would strengthen a mechanistic claim.

questions.prompt: For the simple steady-state mechanism E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, which statement about Km is most accurate?
options: Km is a kinetic parameter; it equals the ES dissociation constant only under additional rapid-equilibrium conditions.
Km is always the equilibrium dissociation constant for substrate binding.
Km is identical to kcat/Km and therefore has units of inverse time.
Km is the concentration of enzyme at which the substrate is half depleted.

feedback.hint: Recall how k-1 and kcat both appear in the steady-state expression for Km.
feedback.solution: Km = (k-1 + kcat)/k1 for the simple mechanism. It approaches the dissociation constant only when product-forming chemistry is sufficiently slow relative to ES dissociation.

questions.prompt: For 520 nm emission and a 1.30 numerical-aperture objective, estimate ideal lateral resolution using d ≈ 0.61 λ/NA. Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Substitute the wavelength in nanometres and keep NA dimensionless.
feedback.solution: d ≈ 0.61 × 520/1.30 ≈ 244 nm. This is an ideal estimate; sampling, specimen optics, signal, and labeling can make practical performance worse.

questions.prompt: Why can a confocal pinhole improve optical sectioning in a thick specimen without guaranteeing better lateral resolution in every image?
options: It rejects much out-of-focus emission, often improving section contrast; lateral resolution still depends on wavelength, numerical aperture, sampling, and the specimen.
It doubles objective numerical aperture regardless of the lens.
It proves that overlapping labels bind directly.
It eliminates photobleaching, background, and specimen movement.

feedback.hint: Separate rejection of out-of-focus signal from the optical factors that set lateral resolution.
feedback.solution: The pinhole rejects much out-of-focus emission and can improve sectioning and contrast, while lateral resolution remains limited by the optical system and measurement conditions.

questions.prompt: Two fluorescence channels overlap within the measured optical resolution. Which conclusion is supported by that observation alone?
options: The detected signals are spatially close at the measured scale under the labeling and analysis conditions; direct binding or causal function requires additional evidence.
The labeled molecules bind directly to each other.
The first protein causes the second protein to enter the compartment.
The overlap proves identical abundance and function in every cell.

feedback.hint: Name the measured spatial relationship, then distinguish it from physical interaction or causal function.
feedback.solution: Optical overlap supports proximity at the assay resolution under those conditions. It does not establish molecular binding, causation, or universal behavior.

questions.prompt: In the synthetic fractionation table, the ER marker recovery is 4% + 18% + 68% + 5%. Enter the recovered percentage with unit.

feedback.hint: Sum the measured marker percentages across every collected fraction.
feedback.solution: 4% + 18% + 68% + 5% = 95% recovery. The remaining 5% is unaccounted for in this assay; it is not proof of biological destruction.

questions.prompt: Interpret the explicitly synthetic fractionation marker panel. Select one response for each analytic criterion.

response_fields.prompt: Fraction interpretation · What does the marker panel support about P2?
options: P2 contains the largest measured share of starting mitochondrial marker, with substantial ER and nuclear marker also present; the table does not establish purity or a concentration-based enrichment factor.
P2 is a pure mitochondrial fraction because it has the largest mitochondrial-marker share.
P2 proves the candidate protein functions inside mitochondria in intact cells.
The panel cannot identify any enrichment.

response_fields.prompt: Recovery accounting · Which calculation gives the ER-marker recovery across collected fractions?
options: Add the ER-marker percentages for P1, P2, P3, and S1 to obtain 95%.
Use only the largest ER-marker value, 68%, as recovery.
Divide ER-marker P2 by mitochondrial-marker P2.
Assume every marker must total exactly 100% even when recovery is incomplete.

response_fields.prompt: Inference boundary · What additional evidence best addresses whether a fractionation pattern reflects in-cell localization?
options: Pair the marker panel and input/recovery checks with an orthogonal intact-cell localization measurement and a claim-matched perturbation control.
Rename P2 after the target organelle.
Load equal total protein without tracking input or fraction volumes.
Treat the pellet label as proof of biological function.

evidence: Identifies P2 as containing the largest measured share of starting mitochondrial marker while acknowledging ER and nuclear marker contamination and the missing concentration denominator.
Sums the ER marker across all collected fractions and reports 95% recovery.
Requests orthogonal intact-cell evidence and controls rather than treating a fraction label as in-cell function.

feedback.hint: Keep enrichment, recovery, purity, and intact-cell localization as separate claims.
feedback.solution: P2 contains the largest measured share of the starting mitochondrial marker but also ER and nuclear markers, so it is not pure. Because protein and volume denominators are absent, the table does not calculate a concentration-based enrichment factor. ER recovery is 95% across all collected fractions. Fractionation alone does not establish intact-cell location or function; combine recovery-aware marker analysis with an orthogonal spatial assay and suitable perturbation controls.

questions.prompt: Which design best tests organelle enrichment while checking contamination and losses during fractionation?
options: Measure the starting input and every collected fraction for several compartment markers, quantify total protein or fraction volume, record recovery, and validate marker specificity in the tested cell system.
Measure one target marker in the intended pellet and infer purity from its intensity.
Compare equal-volume lanes without the starting homogenate.
Use a single organelle marker from a different cell type and assume its localization is unchanged.

feedback.hint: Choose a design that accounts for the input, all outputs, likely contaminants, and recovery.
feedback.solution: A multi-marker panel across the input and all fractions with volume and recovery accounting can support a bounded enrichment claim and expose contamination or losses.

questions.prompt: A template is written 3′-A C G T T A G C-5′. Which complementary DNA product is written with the correct base pairing and polarity?
options: 5′-T G C A A T C G-3′
3′-T G C A A T C G-5′
5′-A G C T T A G C-3′
5′-A C G T T A G C-3′

feedback.hint: Pair A with T and G with C, then remember the new strand runs antiparallel to the template.
feedback.solution: The product is 5′-T G C A A T C G-3′; complementary strands are antiparallel.

questions.prompt: At a fork moving to the right, why is one new DNA strand made continuously while the other is made as Okazaki fragments?
options: Both products must grow 5′ to 3′, but the antiparallel templates point in opposite directions relative to fork movement.
DNA polymerase extends the leading strand 5′ to 3′ and the lagging strand 3′ to 5′.
The lagging strand is made from RNA without later DNA synthesis.
Helicase makes the parental strands parallel at each fork.

feedback.hint: Keep polymerase synthesis direction fixed and compare each template orientation with fork movement.
feedback.solution: DNA polymerase synthesizes both strands 5′ to 3′. The antiparallel geometry makes one strand continuous toward the fork and requires repeated primers and fragments on the other.

questions.prompt: After two generations in light medium, which qualitative result distinguishes semiconservative copying from dispersive copying in an ideal density-labeling experiment?
options: Separate intermediate-density and light-density DNA classes; a single intermediate class after generation one alone is not sufficient.
A single intermediate class that remains the only band at every generation.
A heavy parental class paired only with another heavy class.
A sequence change in every molecule regardless of isotope density.

feedback.hint: Compare the number of density classes after two generations, not just after the first shift.
feedback.solution: The semiconservative model predicts intermediate and light DNA classes after the second generation. Dispersive copying predicts one class that shifts toward light; the first-generation intermediate result alone is compatible with both.

questions.prompt: In an ideal semiconservative model, cells grown in heavy isotope are shifted to light medium for exactly two DNA replication rounds. What percentage of DNA molecules are expected to remain hybrid? Enter a value with unit.

feedback.hint: After the first round all molecules are hybrid; in the second, each hybrid duplex yields one hybrid and one light duplex.
feedback.solution: After the second round, half the DNA molecules are hybrid and half are light: 50%. This is a model prediction for molecule counts, not a measured band intensity.

questions.prompt: Match each lesion or error to a plausible first repair process, then keep the mechanism claim within the stated context.

response_fields.prompt: Bulky lesion · Which pathway is a leading candidate for removing a bulky, helix-distorting UV photoproduct?
options: Nucleotide-excision repair, which removes a short DNA segment containing the lesion.
Mismatch repair, which recognizes every chemical lesion before replication.
Polymerase proofreading, which reverses all completed DNA damage.
Nonhomologous end joining, which excises a UV photoproduct.

response_fields.prompt: Small base lesion · Which pathway commonly begins repair of an oxidized single base?
options: Base-excision repair, initiated by a lesion-recognizing DNA glycosylase.
Homologous recombination, which uses a sister chromatid for every altered base.
Nucleotide-excision repair only after a double-strand break.
Translesion synthesis, which removes the chemical lesion from DNA.

response_fields.prompt: Escaped replication error · Which process can remove a mismatched base pair after it escapes immediate polymerase proofreading?
options: Mismatch repair, which must identify and correct the newly synthesized strand.
Base-excision repair regardless of the mismatch chemistry.
Nucleotide-excision repair of every normal base pair.
DNA ligase alone, without strand selection or excision.

evidence: Selects nucleotide-excision repair for a bulky, helix-distorting UV photoproduct.
Selects base-excision repair for a small oxidized base and recognizes lesion-specific glycosylase initiation.
Selects mismatch repair for an escaped replication mismatch and notes new-strand discrimination.

feedback.hint: Separate an error at the growing 3′ end from a later mismatch or a chemically modified base.
feedback.solution: Proofreading acts at an extending polymerase; mismatch repair can act after an error escapes and targets the new strand; base-excision repair handles many small altered bases; nucleotide-excision repair handles many bulky, helix-distorting lesions. These are candidate routes, not a universal one-pathway-per-lesion rule.

questions.prompt: Interpret the explicitly synthetic, DNA-normalized UV lesion-signal time course. Select one response for each criterion.

response_fields.prompt: Starting burden · What feature makes a difference at 4 h less likely to be explained by unequal initial UV damage?
options: The 0 h lesion-associated signals are similar across the non-targeting, depletion, and rescue groups.
The candidate-depletion group has a higher 4 h signal.
Only the 4 h sample is measured.
The rescue group is omitted from the experiment.

response_fields.prompt: Perturbation evidence · Which pattern supports a role for the candidate factor in the measured signal decline?
options: The 4 h signal remains higher after depletion and moves toward control after a matched rescue.
All groups have exactly zero 0 h signal.
A different cell type is measured only at 4 h.
The depletion effect is inferred from the UV dose alone.

response_fields.prompt: Claim boundary · What does this synthetic lesion-associated signal support by itself?
options: It is consistent with a factor-dependent change in this lesion assay, but does not establish error-free repair or a mutation frequency.
Every lesion was removed without error in every cell type.
A lower signal is a direct count of heritable mutations.
The candidate factor directly catalyzes every nucleotide-excision step.

evidence: Notes that time-zero values are comparable following the matched UV exposure.
Identifies persistent signal after depletion and a matched rescue moving the signal toward control.
Limits the conclusion to a factor-dependent change in the measured assay, not proof of error-free repair or a mutation rate.

feedback.hint: Compare the starting signal before interpreting the four-hour contrast; then state exactly what the rescue and assay measure.
feedback.solution: Similar time-zero values reduce one initial-burden alternative. Higher residual signal after depletion and movement toward control after rescue are consistent with a role for the factor in this assay. The signal is not itself a mutation-frequency measure, and viability, DNA recovery, cell-cycle and orthogonal lesion controls remain important.

questions.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes homologous recombination from nonhomologous end joining at a double-strand break?
options: Homologous recombination copies from a homologous template when available; end joining reconnects ends without an extended homologous template and can involve sequence-changing end processing.
Homologous recombination requires no template, whereas end joining always copies the sister chromatid.
Both routes always restore the exact original sequence.
Nonhomologous end joining is a base-excision pathway for oxidized bases.

feedback.hint: Focus on whether an extended homologous template is used and avoid calling either route universally error-free or error-prone.
feedback.solution: Homologous recombination uses a homologous template and is favored when a sister chromatid is available. End joining does not require that template; end processing can alter sequence, although the outcome depends on context.

questions.prompt: In one cell state, a candidate region has increased accessibility, H3K27ac enrichment, and higher nearby RNA. Which conclusion is best supported before perturbing the region?
options: The measurements are consistent with active regulatory chromatin in this state, but do not establish that the mark or region caused the RNA increase.
H3K27ac directly proves that RNA polymerase initiated transcription at the nearest gene.
The mark establishes that this region is an enhancer for the nearest gene in every cell type.
Higher accessibility proves that every cell in the sample expresses the gene.

feedback.hint: Separate chromatin-state association from a perturbation that tests regulatory function.
feedback.solution: The measurements co-occur and are consistent with active regulatory chromatin in the tested state. They do not establish a causal element or target gene.

questions.prompt: Use the synthetic two-state table in the lesson. Select one response for each criterion.

response_fields.prompt: Accessibility pattern · What changes at the candidate locus while the housekeeping promoter remains similar?
options: Candidate promoter and enhancer accessibility are higher in state A, while the housekeeping value is similar between states.
Only the housekeeping promoter changes and both candidate regions are identical.
All loci are inaccessible in both states.
The table reports absolute nucleosome counts rather than normalized insertion signal.

response_fields.prompt: RNA pattern · How does the candidate gene's RNA relate to the state comparison?
options: Its normalized RNA abundance is higher in state A, co-varying with candidate accessibility.
RNA was measured only in state B.
The RNA value proves the enhancer directly contacts the promoter.
The RNA values are technical PCR wells from a single culture.

response_fields.prompt: Causal boundary · What next step most directly tests endogenous enhancer contribution?
options: Perturb the endogenous element with matched non-targeting and independent perturbations, measure target and nearby RNA, and test rescue where feasible.
Repeat sequencing in the same cultures until read counts are larger.
Assign the enhancer to the nearest gene without perturbing either locus.
Treat cross-state correlation as proof of enhancer causality.

evidence: Identifies higher candidate promoter/enhancer signal and a similar housekeeping-promoter value.
Notes that normalized candidate RNA is higher in state A but remains an association.
Selects controlled endogenous perturbation and claim-matched RNA/rescue evidence.

feedback.hint: Compare both candidate regions, the housekeeping control, and the biological-replicate definition before making a causal claim.
feedback.solution: Candidate accessibility and RNA are higher in state A while housekeeping accessibility is similar. These synthetic measurements support association; controlled perturbation is needed to test contribution.

questions.prompt: An accessibility assay reports greater normalized transposase insertion at a candidate region in one cell state. Which statement describes the measured property most carefully?
options: The region was more susceptible to insertion under the assay conditions; this does not itself measure RNA or prove transcription-factor occupancy.
Every nucleosome was removed and the gene was transcribed in every cell.
The candidate transcription factor directly bound the DNA bases detected by the assay.
The nearest gene is necessarily the functional target of the region.

feedback.hint: Name the assay's physical readout before inferring a mechanism.
feedback.solution: Transposase insertion is an accessibility proxy under defined preparation and normalization. It does not directly quantify RNA, identify a bound factor, or assign a target gene.

questions.prompt: A ChIP experiment saves 1% of starting chromatin as input. The input aliquot reaches threshold at Cq 25 and the immunoprecipitated sample at Cq 22. Assuming ideal doubling efficiency and the same amplicon, estimate the percent input. Enter a value with unit.

feedback.hint: Use 100 × input fraction × 2^(Cq input aliquot − Cq IP).
feedback.solution: 100 × 0.01 × 2^(25 − 22) = 8% input under the stated ideal-efficiency assumption.

questions.prompt: Choose the control that best addresses each distinct ChIP-qPCR question.

response_fields.prompt: Starting material · Which sample provides a pre-immunoprecipitation reference for input chromatin?
options: An aliquot of fragmented chromatin saved before immunoprecipitation, with its fraction recorded.
A no-template qPCR well.
A promoter-only reporter plasmid.
A second technical PCR well from the IP.

response_fields.prompt: Nonspecific pull-down · Which control estimates recovery unrelated to the target antibody?
options: A matched IgG or mock immunoprecipitation.
The input aliquot alone.
A known positive qPCR locus alone.
A no-template qPCR well alone.

response_fields.prompt: Locus/PCR specificity · Which set tests expected enrichment, locus specificity, and PCR contamination?
options: A known positive locus, an unrelated negative locus, and a no-template qPCR control.
Three PCR wells from one culture and no target region.
Input and IgG only, with no locus controls or PCR blank.
A promoterless reporter and a rescue construct.

evidence: Selects pre-IP chromatin and records the saved fraction.
Selects matched IgG or mock IP to estimate nonspecific recovery.
Includes positive/negative loci and a no-template PCR control.

feedback.hint: Match each control to the stage it interrogates: starting chromatin, IP background, locus specificity, or PCR.
feedback.solution: Input controls starting-material representation; matched IgG or mock IP estimates nonspecific recovery; positive and negative loci test locus-level behavior; no-template qPCR checks amplification contamination or artifacts.

questions.prompt: Interpret the synthetic reporter table while keeping the construct's limits explicit.

response_fields.prompt: Sequence contribution · What does the matched wild-type versus motif-disrupted comparison support?
options: The motif contributes to reporter output in this construct and condition; mutation alone does not establish endogenous regulation.
The motif is necessary for endogenous expression in every tissue.
The mutant proves that the transcription factor directly contacts the motif.
Any difference is necessarily caused by altered cell viability.

response_fields.prompt: Normalization · What condition is needed before a co-transfected reference reporter is used as a normalizer?
options: The reference must be stable and not itself changed by treatment, alongside matched DNA and viability checks.
The reference must use the same enhancer and show a large treatment effect.
A technical well can replace independent transfections.
The promoter-only construct can be omitted.

response_fields.prompt: Endogenous limit · Which evidence most directly strengthens a claim about the native locus?
options: A controlled endogenous motif perturbation with matched controls, target/neighbor RNA measurement, and rescue where feasible.
A second ChIP measurement at the same locus only.
A larger plasmid copy number in the same transfection.
Assigning the nearest gene based on distance.

evidence: Limits the motif interpretation to contribution to the reporter construct in the tested condition.
Checks that the reference is treatment-stable and considers matched DNA and viability.
Chooses controlled endogenous perturbation and target/neighbor RNA with rescue where feasible.

feedback.hint: Separate a construct-specific sequence effect from a native-locus mechanism.
feedback.solution: The synthetic wild-type reporter exceeds promoter-only and motif disruption reduces signal in this construct. Reference normalization is valid only if the reference is unaffected. Native-locus perturbation and endogenous RNA/rescue are needed for a stronger gene-regulation claim.

questions.prompt: ChIP-qPCR enrichment is observed at a distal element and the nearest gene has higher RNA in the same cell type. Which next step most directly tests whether the endogenous element contributes to that gene's transcription?
options: Perturb the endogenous element with independent guides or edits, matched non-targeting and nearby controls, then measure target and neighboring RNA and test rescue where feasible.
Repeat ChIP-qPCR with more PCR wells from the same chromatin sample.
Assign the nearest gene as the target because the enhancer is closest.
Repeat a plasmid reporter without changing its sequence or measuring endogenous RNA.

feedback.hint: Choose an intervention on the native element and a measurement of native transcription.
feedback.solution: Controlled endogenous perturbation followed by target and neighboring RNA measurements tests the proposed link more directly. Independent perturbations and rescue help address off-target and cell-state alternatives.

questions.prompt: A perturbation changes the fraction of two mature RNA isoforms, while a shared-exon assay and an intron-containing precursor assay remain similar. Which conclusion is best supported?

feedback.hint: Separate the measured mature-RNA mixture from the amount of transcript entering and remaining in the RNA pool.
feedback.solution: The data support a change in the measured isoform mixture without a large change in the shared mature signal or measured precursor. They do not identify direct action at a splice site or exclude every stability and cell-state alternative.

options: The measured mature isoform composition changed; the data alone do not show that total transcription changed.
Transcription must have doubled because one isoform increased.
The protein encoded by the included isoform is necessarily more active.
The splice regulator directly binds the measured splice site because the isoform fraction changed.

variants.prompt: A splice-factor perturbation shifts junction-specific counts between two mature isoforms, while a shared-exon signal is similar. Which statement best fits these measurements?
options: The isoform mixture changed in the assay; this does not by itself demonstrate altered transcription or protein function.
Equal shared-exon signal proves that every RNA-processing step was unchanged.
The larger isoform count proves direct binding of the factor to that RNA sequence.
A change in one junction signal proves that cell viability fell.

feedback.hint: Name the RNA species measured by each assay before making a mechanistic claim.
feedback.solution: Junction-specific assays report isoform evidence; a shared-exon assay reports a common region. Neither alone proves direct binding, transcription rate, or protein function.

variants.prompt: A cell has similar intron-containing precursor signal and total shared-exon RNA after a perturbation, but exon-junction counts move in opposite directions. What does this pattern most directly suggest?
options: A shift in the measured mature isoform composition, subject to assay and cell-state limits.
A proven increase in transcription of the entire gene.
A proven increase in total protein activity.
A direct measurement of RNA degradation rate.

feedback.hint: Opposing junction counts with a similar shared signal describe composition more directly than total output.
feedback.solution: The measurements are consistent with altered isoform composition. Nascent-RNA, decay, rescue, and orthogonal sequence assays would address other possible mechanisms.

questions.prompt: For the synthetic splice-factor dataset, choose an interpretation and two design checks that distinguish isoform evidence from transcription, assay artifact, and reagent-specific effects.

evidence: Names an isoform-composition shift and avoids inferring transcription or protein activity.
Selects independent perturbations and a rescue where feasible.
Selects a no-reverse-transcriptase control for genomic DNA contamination.

feedback.hint: State what the junction and shared-region assays measure, then choose one perturbation-specificity check and one RT-PCR control.
feedback.solution: The pattern supports a measured isoform-composition shift with similar shared and precursor signals. Independent perturbations plus rescue address reagent-specific effects; a no-reverse-transcriptase reaction tests genomic-DNA carryover.

response_fields.prompt: Interpretation: which statement is limited to the measured RNA evidence?
options: The measured isoform proportions shifted while the shared mature and precursor signals were similar.
The perturbation increased transcription of the whole gene.
The altered isoform necessarily produces a more active protein.

response_fields.prompt: Perturbation control: which design most directly addresses a reagent-specific effect?
options: Use independent perturbation reagents and a perturbation-resistant rescue where feasible.
Add more PCR wells from the same RNA preparation.
Use only the isoform with the largest count.

response_fields.prompt: RNA assay control: which control checks for genomic DNA carried into a reverse-transcription PCR?
options: A no-reverse-transcriptase reaction.
A positive reporter construct.
A matched IgG immunoprecipitation.

questions.prompt: In the synthetic splice-factor depletion data, the skipped isoform has 60 measured counts and the included isoform has 30. What percentage of these two measured mature isoforms is skipped? Enter a value with unit. Round to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Divide the skipped count by the sum of the two measured mature isoform counts, then multiply by 100.
feedback.solution: 60 / (60 + 30) x 100 = 66.7%. This is the fraction among the two measured forms, not among every RNA molecule in the cell.

questions.prompt: During eukaryotic translation, a stop codon enters the ribosomal A site. Which event most directly terminates synthesis of that polypeptide?

feedback.hint: Stop codons are recognized by a release factor rather than by an aminoacyl-tRNA carrying the next amino acid.
feedback.solution: A release factor recognizes the stop codon and promotes release of the peptide from the tRNA. It does not add another amino acid specified by that stop codon.

options: A release factor promotes hydrolysis of the peptide-tRNA linkage and ribosome recycling.
A matching aminoacyl-tRNA adds an amino acid encoded by the stop codon.
RNA polymerase removes the final codon from the mRNA.
The ribosome moves backward by one codon and restarts elongation.

questions.prompt: A background-corrected, labeled protein signal is 80 units at the start of a chase and 40 units after 4 hours. Assuming first-order decay over this interval, estimate the protein half-life. Enter a value in hours.

feedback.hint: A first-order half-life is the elapsed time for the background-corrected labeled signal to fall to one half of its initial value.
feedback.solution: The signal falls from 80 to 40 units in 4 hours, exactly one half under the stated model; the estimated half-life is 4.0 h. A robust experiment would use multiple points, replicates, and a validated decay model.

questions.prompt: In the synthetic dataset, target mRNA and estimated protein half-life are similar across conditions, while nascent protein and steady-state protein fall after regulator depletion and move toward control after rescue. Select the best model-level inference, a useful follow-up, and a bounded conclusion.

evidence: Selects lower synthesis per measured RNA while half-life is similar.
Pairs ribosome-engagement evidence with target RNA.
Uses consistent-with language and does not claim direct initiation action.

feedback.hint: Compare the measured RNA, synthesis, and decay dimensions separately before selecting a mechanism.
feedback.solution: The results are consistent with reduced synthesis per measured RNA in the tested conditions. Ribosome-engagement measurements paired with target RNA may refine the mechanism. Rescue does not establish direct binding or direct action at initiation.

response_fields.prompt: Mechanistic inference: which broad model term is most directly supported as lower?
options: The synthesis rate per measured transcript, while the measured half-life is similar.
The first-order degradation constant, because the steady protein is lower.
The mature target mRNA abundance, because the protein is lower.

response_fields.prompt: Follow-up: which measurement could help test ribosome engagement while retaining a matched RNA measurement?
options: A controlled polysome profile or ribosome-footprint assay paired with target mRNA.
A larger steady-state protein gel from the same lysate only.
A promoter-only plasmid reporter with no translation readout.

response_fields.prompt: Claim boundary: what conclusion is warranted by the synthetic measurements?
options: They are consistent with reduced synthesis per measured mRNA in these conditions, but do not prove direct action at initiation.
They prove that the candidate regulator physically binds the target mRNA.
They establish that the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway is inactive.

questions.prompt: Select the replication unit, a concern about inhibitor-based turnover measurements, and the strongest warranted interpretation of a rescue experiment.

evidence: Counts an independently grown and processed culture as a biological replicate.
Names stress signaling or viability as potential inhibitor-related confounds.
States that rescue supports involvement without proving direct catalysis or universal action.

feedback.hint: Keep independent cultures, treatment effects on cell state, and direct molecular evidence distinct.
feedback.solution: Independent cultures are biological replicates. Chase inhibitors can alter stress and viability. A rescue supports involvement in the tested system but does not alone prove direct action.

response_fields.prompt: Replication: what should count as the biological replicate in this cell-culture comparison?
options: An independently grown and processed culture.
Each qPCR well from the same culture.
Each sequencing read from one culture.

response_fields.prompt: Turnover assay: what is an essential concern in an inhibitor-based chase?
options: The inhibitor can alter stress signaling or viability, so matched controls and cell-state monitoring matter.
Any inhibitor guarantees perfectly first-order degradation.
A single endpoint identifies which protease degraded the protein.

response_fields.prompt: Rescue interpretation: what does restoration after factor rescue support?
options: Involvement of the factor in the tested system, while direct molecular action still requires additional evidence.
Proof that the factor directly catalyzes translation initiation.
Proof that all cell types will show the same response.

questions.prompt: Which action is directly performed during spliceosome-mediated processing of a typical eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
options: The spliceosome helps recognize splice sites, remove an intron through a lariat intermediate, and ligate selected exons.
The spliceosome adds a 7-methylguanosine cap to the 5-prime end.
The spliceosome translates each codon into an amino acid.
The spliceosome appends a poly(A) tail to every eukaryotic RNA molecule.

feedback.hint: Separate intron removal and exon joining from capping, translation, and 3-prime end processing.
feedback.solution: The spliceosome catalyzes splice-site selection and intron removal with exon ligation. Capping and polyadenylation are distinct RNA-processing operations; ribosomes perform translation.

questions.prompt: A parent is heterozygous A/a and the other parent is a/a. Under ordinary Mendelian segregation, what is the probability that a child inherits allele A?

feedback.hint: Calculate transmission from the heterozygous parent's two alleles; phenotype probability is a separate conditional step.
feedback.solution: Each gamete from an A/a parent carries A with probability 1/2. This is the allele-transmission probability, not the probability of a phenotype.

questions.prompt: One parent is A/a and the other is a/a. A defined phenotype has 80% penetrance among A/a carriers by age 40 and is absent among noncarriers under this simplified model. What is the predicted probability that one child meets the phenotype definition by age 40? Enter a percentage.

feedback.hint: Multiply the chance of inheriting A by the conditional phenotype probability among carriers.
feedback.solution: P(A/a) = 0.5 and P(phenotype | A/a) = 0.8, so 0.5 x 0.8 = 0.40 or 40.0%. This depends on the stated simplified assumptions and age.

questions.prompt: In a synthetic family, a candidate allele is confirmed in five adult relatives; four meet a prespecified phenotype threshold, and the fifth is age 22 while the condition is usually assessed after age 40. Interpret the fraction, the younger carrier, and the limits of the pedigree.

response_fields.prompt: Descriptive fraction: among the five observed carriers, four meet the stated threshold. What fraction is observed?
options: 4/5, or 80% in this small observed group.
1/2, or 50% by Mendelian inheritance.
5/5, because all five carry the allele.

response_fields.prompt: Age: one unaffected carrier is 22, below the usual assessment age of 40. How should this observation be treated?
options: The person is not yet fully observed for an age-dependent phenotype; record age and follow-up.
The person proves complete nonpenetrance at every age.
The person's genotype should be changed to noncarrier.

response_fields.prompt: Inference: what is the strongest bounded interpretation of 4/5 in a referred family?
options: It is a descriptive fraction in this small, ascertained family, not a population or lifelong penetrance estimate.
It establishes exactly 80% penetrance for every ancestry and age.
It proves the allele alone caused all four phenotypes.

evidence: Reports four of five, or 80%, as a descriptive fraction in this sample.
Treats the younger carrier as not fully observed through the usual assessment age.
Avoids generalizing a small ascertained family fraction to lifelong population penetrance.

feedback.hint: Separate the observed sample fraction from the genotype-transmission model, and ask whether every carrier has passed the relevant assessment age.
feedback.solution: Four of five observed carriers meet the threshold, but this is a descriptive 80% in a small referred family. The younger carrier is age-censored for a condition usually assessed after 40. Ascertainment, phenocopies, family environment, and other variants limit generalization.

questions.prompt: A candidate allele is more common in cases than controls, but cases and controls were recruited from populations with different ancestry composition. Which concern most directly challenges a causal interpretation?
options: Population stratification may confound the association even if the allele is not causal.
The result proves the allele directly changes protein function.
Different ancestry composition is irrelevant whenever the sample is large.
The allele must be a de novo mutation in every case.

feedback.hint: Ask whether ancestry is associated with both allele frequency and the sampling or phenotype process.
feedback.solution: Population structure can associate allele frequency with case status through ancestry or recruitment differences. An association is not proof that this base change causes the phenotype; family-based analysis, ancestry-aware design, replication, and functional tests address different alternatives.

questions.prompt: A missense annotation predicts a changed amino acid. What does the annotation establish by itself?
options: The variant is predicted to change an amino acid; effect and phenotype remain to be measured.
The variant necessarily causes disease in every carrier.
The protein's catalytic activity is known to be zero.
The phenotype is proven to arise through altered splicing.

feedback.hint: Separate the sequence consequence from RNA, protein, cellular, and organism-level measurements.
feedback.solution: The annotation describes a sequence-level consequence and suggests hypotheses. It does not establish a measured molecular effect, a cellular phenotype, or clinical causality.

questions.prompt: Interpret the synthetic mock-edited, variant-knock-in, and variant-corrected data. Choose the directly measured protein-level result, what correction contributes, and a follow-up that distinguishes synthesis from turnover.

response_fields.prompt: Data interpretation: RNA and activity per measured protein are similar, protein amount per viable cell is lower, and the cell-response index is higher in the knock-in clones. Which molecular change is most directly observed?
options: Lower measured Protein X amount per viable cell, with similar measured RNA and specific activity.
A proven decrease in catalytic activity per Protein X molecule.
A proven increase in transcript production.

response_fields.prompt: Reversibility: what does the variant-corrected group add?
options: Evidence that measured protein amount and cell response move toward reference in the tested corrected clones.
Proof that no clone-specific or editing-related alternative exists.
Proof of a tissue-level phenotype in an organism.

response_fields.prompt: Next mechanism test: which paired measurements best separate lower synthesis from faster protein removal?
options: A short-pulse nascent-protein assay and a multi-time-point protein pulse-chase, with matched controls.
One additional steady-state immunoblot from the same lysate.
A larger number of technical wells for the same endpoint.

evidence: Identifies lower protein amount per viable cell while avoiding a claim of lower specific activity.
States that correction moves tested measurements toward reference without excluding every clone/edit alternative.
Pairs a nascent-protein measurement with a multi-time-point turnover assay.

feedback.hint: Compare RNA, protein amount per viable cell, activity per measured protein, and the cell response as separate columns.
feedback.solution: The synthetic table shows lower Protein X amount per viable cell with similar measured RNA and specific activity, plus a cell-response shift. Correction moves the readouts toward reference, supporting a variant-associated effect in these clones. Pulse labeling and a controlled turnover time course can separate synthesis from removal, but do not by themselves prove organism-level causality.

questions.prompt: Select one control for clone/edit effects, one denominator for a specific-activity claim, and one appropriate limit on a rescued cell phenotype.

response_fields.prompt: Editing control: which design addresses clone-specific effects?
options: Compare multiple independently derived, sequence-checked clones with mock-edited controls.
Measure many wells from one selected clone only.
Assume the editing reagent changes no other sequence or cell property.

response_fields.prompt: Enzyme claim: which denominator is needed to compare catalytic activity per Protein X molecule?
options: Validated measured amount of Protein X under matched assay conditions.
Total culture volume without measuring protein.
The number of sequencing reads in the variant sample.

response_fields.prompt: Claim boundary: what does a rescued cell-culture phenotype establish?
options: A reversible effect in the tested cellular system that supports involvement, not an organism-level or clinical conclusion by itself.
Proof that the variant causes the same trait in every tissue and person.
A complete pathogenicity classification.

evidence: Uses independent sequence-checked clones and mock-edited controls.
Uses measured Protein X amount as the activity denominator.
Does not generalize a cell-culture rescue to all tissues or a clinical classification.

feedback.hint: Match each claim to the denominator or control that tests it, and keep cell culture separate from organism-level inference.
feedback.solution: Independent clones and mock edits address different edit/clone alternatives. Protein amount is required for activity per Protein X. A rescue supports reversibility in the tested cells but does not establish a universal organismal or clinical effect.

questions.prompt: Under the idealized single-site equilibrium model, free ligand is 1 nM and Kd is 4 nM. What fraction of receptors is predicted to be occupied? Enter a fraction from 0 to 1, not a percentage.

feedback.hint: Use θ = [L]free / (Kd + [L]free) and keep the output as a fraction.
feedback.solution: θ = 1/(4 + 1) = 0.20. This idealized binding estimate is not a prediction that the cell response is 20% of maximum.

questions.prompt: Which sequence is one common route from an activated receptor tyrosine kinase toward ERK?
options: Gαs activates adenylyl cyclase, cyclic AMP activates PKA, then PKA becomes Ras.
Receptor phosphotyrosines recruit adaptors that can activate Ras-GTP, followed by a RAF–MEK–ERK kinase relay.
A receptor directly converts extracellular ligand into ERK RNA without intracellular intermediates.
Ligand binding necessarily causes every receptor class to activate the same kinase sequence.

feedback.hint: Follow the adaptor and small-GTPase connection in a common RTK example.
feedback.solution: One common RTK route uses phosphotyrosine docking proteins to connect receptor activation to Ras and the RAF–MEK–ERK cascade. Other receptors and cell contexts can use different branches.

questions.prompt: In a synthetic assay, pERK signal is 36 relative units in ligand-stimulated cells and 4 relative units in matched vehicle controls at the same collection time. What is the stimulated-to-vehicle fold change?

feedback.hint: Divide the stimulated index by the specified comparison index.
feedback.solution: 36/4 = 9. This assay ratio describes the measured pERK index; it does not state receptor occupancy or a cell-fate change.

questions.prompt: Interpret the synthetic week-11 phospho-ERK time course after a two-minute ligand pulse or continued exposure.

response_fields.prompt: Time-course shape · Which description best matches the table?
options: Both conditions return to vehicle by 10 minutes.
The pulse signal declines toward baseline, while continued-exposure signal remains elevated at 60 minutes.
The pulse condition has no early signal, while continued exposure first activates at 60 minutes.

response_fields.prompt: Early peak · What is the bounded comparison at 2 minutes?
options: The two reported means are similar at 2 minutes; the table does not establish identical receptor occupancy.
The receptors must have equal affinity and abundance in both conditions.
The table proves the later cell fates are equal.

response_fields.prompt: Claim boundary · Which conclusion follows directly from this readout?
options: The conditions differ in the measured phospho-ERK trajectory; later fate requires a separate outcome assay.
The continued condition causes differentiation in every cell type.
The pulse condition triggers apoptosis because its signal declines.

rubric.criterion: Compare response duration under the stated exposure schedules
evidence: Identifies a decline after the pulse and a sustained elevated signal during continued exposure.

rubric.criterion: Use the measured early values without inferring unmeasured binding
evidence: Notes similar 2-minute phospho-ERK values and does not claim equal affinity or occupancy.

rubric.criterion: Keep biochemical and cell-fate outcomes separate
evidence: Limits the conclusion to the measured phospho-ERK trajectory and calls for a separate fate assay.

feedback.hint: Separate the measured signaling variable, the exposure schedule, the intervention target, and the scope of the claim.
feedback.solution: The synthetic means show similar early pERK values and a longer elevated trajectory under continued exposure. A phosphorylation trace does not establish a later transcriptional or cell-fate outcome.

questions.prompt: Receptor inhibition lowers pERK. Constitutively active MEK restores pERK in the tested cells. Interpret the bypass evidence.

response_fields.prompt: Pathway position · What does the rescue most directly support?
options: The receptor is the only upstream influence on every cellular pathway.
The intervention restored every receptor function to its natural state.
Active MEK can bypass the receptor block to restore the measured pERK state in these cells.

response_fields.prompt: Inference limit · Which additional statement is justified?
options: An artificial bypass does not by itself establish normal physiological sufficiency or restored cell fate.
Restored pERK proves the cells differentiated normally.
Overexpression eliminates all off-target and expression-level concerns.

rubric.criterion: Interpret the bypass at the measured downstream node
evidence: Describes restoration of measured pERK by the MEK bypass in the tested cells.
Separates biochemical bypass from normal physiology and cell-fate outcomes.

feedback.hint: Separate the measured signaling variable, the exposure schedule, the intervention target, and the scope of the claim.
feedback.solution: The bypass supports that active MEK can restore the specified pERK measurement under these conditions. It does not show normal physiological sufficiency, restoration of every receptor branch, or cell-fate rescue.

questions.prompt: A ligand-induced pERK signal declines. Select follow-ups that distinguish ligand availability, receptor adaptation, induced feedback, and alternative explanations.

response_fields.prompt: Ligand-depletion test · Which comparison addresses whether ligand availability explains the decline?
options: Use a matched medium exchange without measuring or replacing ligand.
Maintain or replenish ligand at a controlled concentration with matched medium-change and vehicle controls.
Increase the number of technical wells only in the declining condition.

response_fields.prompt: Receptor-adaptation test · Which paired measurement is informative?
options: Measure matched surface and total receptor abundance across the signaling time course.
Measure only the final pERK value in one dish.
Replace receptor measurements with a later morphology photograph.

response_fields.prompt: Induced-feedback test · Which sequence supports a candidate feedback contribution?
options: Assume any delayed response is feedback without measuring an intermediate.
Measure candidate expression only once after the signal has ended.
Measure candidate abundance or activity over time, perturb it with a matched control, and test a specific rescue.

response_fields.prompt: Alternative explanation · Which control helps detect a cell-state alternative?
options: Use technical replicate count as a substitute for cell health.
Measure viability and cell number at matched times alongside signaling.
Assume equal starting density guarantees equal viability throughout.

rubric.criterion: Control the ligand input while testing depletion
evidence: Uses controlled ligand maintenance or replenishment and matched medium-change controls.
Compares surface and total receptor at matched time points.

rubric.criterion: Test the feedback candidate with a temporal and causal chain
evidence: Combines time-resolved candidate measurement, controlled perturbation, and a specific rescue.

rubric.criterion: Check cell-state alternatives at the measured times
evidence: Measures viability and cell number alongside the signaling readout.

feedback.hint: Separate the measured signaling variable, the exposure schedule, the intervention target, and the scope of the claim.
feedback.solution: Different hypotheses need different measurements: controlled ligand input addresses depletion, time-matched surface and total receptor address receptor availability, and a temporally measured candidate perturbation with rescue tests feedback contribution. Viability and cell count help identify state changes. No single item alone proves a unique mechanism.

questions.prompt: A small-molecule inhibitor reduces pERK. Which next result most strengthens the claim that the targeted pathway component contributes, while addressing a different intervention-specific alternative?
options: More technical wells with the same inhibitor and no target-engagement measurement.
A second endpoint at the same time using the same compound concentration.
An orthogonal controlled genetic perturbation with target-engagement evidence and a specific rescue of a prespecified readout.
A later cell image chosen after inspecting which field looks most different.

feedback.hint: Ask whether a different intervention changes the predicted node, and whether restoring that component rescues the prespecified readout.
feedback.solution: An orthogonal perturbation with target engagement and specific rescue can address different off-target or attribution alternatives. The conclusion must still be limited to the tested readout, cells, and conditions.

questions.prompt: A uniform force of 12 μN is applied across an original area of 3 × 10⁻⁹ m². Under the stated uniform-loading approximation, what is the engineering stress in Pa?

feedback.hint: Convert microNewtons to Newtons, then divide force by area.
feedback.solution: 12 μN = 12 × 10⁻⁶ N; σ = F/A = (12 × 10⁻⁶)/(3 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.0 × 10³ Pa. This is stress under the stated geometry, not a modulus.

questions.prompt: Which statement best compares the common roles of the three major cytoskeletal filament systems?
options: Intermediate filaments commonly provide tissue-dependent mechanical resilience; microtubules organize transport tracks and intracellular structure; actin contributes to cortex, protrusion, and contractile networks.
All three systems are static structural rods with identical molecular subunits and mechanical functions.
Actin uniquely transports every organelle, microtubules only reinforce epithelial sheets, and intermediate filaments polymerize into membrane channels.
Microtubules and actin are covalent polymers, while intermediate filaments never remodel after cell division.

feedback.hint: Match each filament to its common structure, dynamics, and cellular tasks; the systems also interact.
feedback.solution: Actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments have distinct common roles and mechanics. All are associated with accessory proteins and can reorganize in living cells.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts one common cell–matrix linkage with a cell–cell linkage?
options: Cadherins bind most collagen directly and connect only to microtubules.
Integrins bind many ECM ligands and connect through adaptors to cytoskeletal structures; cadherins can connect neighboring cells through their own associated proteins.
Integrins are extracellular matrix fibers that have no transmembrane or signaling role.
Focal adhesions and desmosomes are the same junction measured with different stains.

feedback.hint: Name the ligand location first: outside matrix versus a neighboring cell.
feedback.solution: Integrins are transmembrane matrix receptors that can connect through adaptors to the cytoskeleton. Cadherins mediate selected cell–cell contacts and link to intracellular partners. The junctions are not interchangeable.

questions.prompt: Interpret the explicitly synthetic hydrogel dataset in the lesson, in which ligand density and culture conditions were matched across measured substrate moduli.

response_fields.prompt: Measured trend · What pattern is reported from 2 to 30 kPa?
options: Both the nuclear YAP-positive fraction and traction-force index increase across the three synthetic conditions.
Only the soft condition has nonzero readouts.
